unit.title: Analyse and interpret workforce development trends

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: An HR manager at a Montego Bay hotel group is asked to analyse workforce development trends. What is she mainly being asked to study?

The personal habits of the senior staff
Changes over time in skills, jobs and labour
The cost and design of new staff uniforms

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What word names a long-term pattern of change in data over time, such as a steady rise in demand for a skill?
What four-letter abbreviation is used for the Planning Institute of Jamaica?

A firm's staff numbers rose from 250 to 300. What is the percentage increase?

essays.stem: Explain what is meant by workforce development trends, and why a manager in a Jamaican organisation needs to analyse them. Give three examples of current trends.
essays.modelAnswer: Workforce development trends are long-term patterns of change in the supply of workers, the skills they have, the jobs available and the way work is done. They are found by studying data over several years, both inside the organisation and in the wider labour market. A manager needs to analyse them because they affect whether the organisation will have the right people with the right skills in future. If trends are spotted early, the organisation can plan recruitment, training and retention in good time instead of reacting to a crisis, and it can make better use of its training budget. One current trend is the migration of skilled workers, such as nurses and teachers, to jobs overseas, which creates shortages at home. A second is the spread of automation and digital tools, which removes some routine jobs and creates demand for digital and analytical skills. A third is the growth of flexible patterns of work, such as remote, hybrid and gig work, which changes how staff expect to work and how they are managed.
markingPoints: Clear definition of workforce development trends
Explains why analysis matters for planning skills and people
First relevant example explained
Second relevant example explained
Third relevant example explained

essays.stem: Describe the sources of information you would use to analyse workforce trends in Jamaica's tourism sector, and explain how you would judge how reliable each one is.
essays.modelAnswer: I would use national sources first, such as the Labour Force Survey from the Statistical Institute of Jamaica for employment by industry, and the Planning Institute of Jamaica's yearly Economic and Social Survey for sector trends. I would add reports from tourism industry associations and the national training agency on skills needs, visitor arrival figures, news of new hotels and attractions, and job advertisements to see which skills employers are seeking. Inside my own organisation I would use HR records on staff numbers, ages, turnover, vacancies and training. To judge reliability, I would ask who produced the information and whether they are independent and expert, and whether they have a reason to present it in a certain way. I would check how recent the data is, how it was collected, how large the sample was and whether it covers the whole sector or only part. I would compare sources to see whether they agree, and treat claims without clear evidence, such as some news or social media posts, with caution. I would record the source and date of every figure I use.
markingPoints: Names national statistical and planning sources
Names industry, training or job advert sources
Includes internal HR data
Gives clear tests of reliability: author, date, method, sample
Compares sources and records them

essays.stem: A business process outsourcing firm in Montego Bay had 600 staff in 2023, 660 in 2024 and 750 in 2025. Leavers were 90 in 2023, 120 in 2024 and 150 in 2025. Using each year's staff number as the base, work out the growth in staff from one year to the next and the turnover rate for each year. Then describe the trends and their implications for workforce development.
essays.modelAnswer: Staff grew by 60, from 600 to 660, between 2023 and 2024, which is 60 divided by 600, or 10%. Between 2024 and 2025 staff grew by 90, from 660 to 750, which is 90 divided by 660, or about 13.6%. So growth is speeding up. The turnover rate was 90 divided by 600, or 15%, in 2023; 120 divided by 660, or about 18.2%, in 2024; and 150 divided by 750, or 20%, in 2025. Turnover is also rising every year. Together the figures show a fast-growing firm that is losing a growing share of its staff, so it has to recruit far more people than its growth alone would suggest: in 2025 it needed about 240 new hires to grow by 90. This raises recruitment and training costs and may affect service quality. The firm should find out why people leave, through exit interviews and surveys, and act on pay, shift patterns, supervision or career paths. It should also build a steady pipeline of trained recruits, for example through partnerships with training providers, and develop team leaders from within.
markingPoints: Growth correctly worked out: 10% then about 13.6%
Turnover correctly worked out: 15%, about 18.2% and 20%
Describes both trends correctly
Explains implications such as recruitment, cost or quality
Recommends sensible workforce development actions

essays.stem: Explain how automation and digital technology are changing jobs and skills in Jamaican workplaces, and recommend how an employer should respond.
essays.modelAnswer: Automation and digital technology are taking over many routine tasks, such as data entry, simple bookkeeping, cash handling and some customer queries, which are now done by software, online services, self-service machines and chatbots. At the same time, new tasks and jobs are growing, such as analysing data, managing online sales and social media, supporting customers through digital channels and maintaining systems. Even jobs that remain are changing, as most staff now need basic digital skills, and many need to work with data. This can leave some workers at risk of losing their jobs if they are not retrained, and it can widen gaps between people who have digital access and skills and those who do not. An employer should first study which of its roles and tasks are likely to change over the next few years. It should then plan upskilling for staff whose jobs are changing and reskilling for those whose jobs may disappear, consult staff early and honestly, and include digital skills in recruitment and induction. Partnerships with training providers can help, and the plan should be reviewed each year as technology moves on.
markingPoints: Explains routine tasks being automated with examples
Explains new jobs and skills being created
Notes risks for workers or skills gaps
Recommends analysing roles and planning upskilling and reskilling
Includes consultation, partnerships or regular review

essays.stem: The migration of skilled workers overseas concerns many Jamaican employers. Analyse its effects on an organisation such as a hospital or a school, and recommend how the organisation should respond.
essays.modelAnswer: When experienced nurses or teachers leave for jobs overseas, the organisation loses skill, knowledge and leadership that took years to build. Vacancies may stay open for months, so the remaining staff carry heavier workloads, which can lead to stress, more absence and further resignations. Service quality may fall, for example longer waiting times in a hospital or larger classes in a school. The organisation also loses the money it spent training these staff, and it must pay to recruit and train replacements, who are often less experienced. To respond, the organisation should first measure the problem: how many leave, from which roles and why, using exit interviews and surveys. It can then act on the reasons it can influence, such as working conditions, workload, recognition, flexible hours, career paths and professional development, while working with the relevant ministry on pay where it is set centrally. It should plan succession and train more staff than it needs to allow for losses, use mentoring to pass on knowledge, and keep in touch with those who leave, as some may return later with valuable experience.
markingPoints: Explains loss of skills and knowledge
Explains effects on workload, morale and service
Notes costs of replacing staff
Recommends measuring causes and improving retention
Recommends succession, training pipeline or knowledge transfer

essays.stem: Explain the difference between correlation and causation, and why it matters when interpreting workforce data. Use a workplace example.
essays.modelAnswer: Correlation means that two measures tend to move together: when one is high, the other tends to be high (or low). Causation means that a change in one measure actually brings about a change in the other. Two things can be correlated without one causing the other, because a third factor may affect both, or the link may be chance. For example, an analyst may find that branches of a retail chain where staff receive more training hours also have lower staff turnover. It is tempting to conclude that training causes staff to stay. However, the branches with more training may also have better managers, who both arrange training and treat staff well, and it may be the management that keeps staff. It could even work the other way: branches with stable staff find it easier to release people for training. This matters because decisions based on a false cause waste money and miss the real problem. Before acting, the analyst should look for other factors, compare similar branches, use more than one source, and where possible test the idea, for example through a pilot.
markingPoints: Defines correlation correctly
Defines causation correctly
Explains third factors, chance or reverse cause
Gives a relevant workplace example
Explains why it matters and how to check

essays.stem: Describe how you would present your findings on workforce trends to a senior management team so that they lead to decisions.
essays.modelAnswer: Senior managers have little time, so I would start with a one-page summary that states the three or four most important trends, what they mean for the organisation and the decisions I am asking for. I would then present the evidence for each trend clearly, using a few well-labelled charts rather than long tables: for example a line graph of turnover over five years and a bar chart of the age profile by department. Each chart would have a short heading that says what it shows, such as "Turnover has risen every year since 2022". I would explain the limits of the data honestly, such as small samples or old figures, so that managers can judge how much weight to give it. For each trend I would set out the implications, such as the number of retirements expected in key posts, and offer options with their costs and benefits, then a clear recommendation. I would link the recommendations to the strategic plan and budget. Detailed tables and methods would go in an appendix. Finally, I would allow time for questions and agree the next steps and who will take them.
markingPoints: Opens with a short summary of key trends and decisions needed
Uses clear, well-labelled charts
States the limits of the data honestly
Sets out implications, options and recommendations linked to strategy
Allows questions and agrees next steps

essays.stem: Use a PESTLE analysis to identify workforce development trends that could affect a large hardware and building supplies company in Jamaica over the next five years.
essays.modelAnswer: Under political factors, government plans for housing and road building could increase demand and the need for staff, while changes in public spending could reduce it. Under economic factors, interest rates, construction activity and the cost of living affect sales and the wages staff expect, and a strong job market may make skilled staff harder to keep. Under social factors, an ageing group of experienced counter and warehouse staff, the migration of skilled workers overseas, and young people's wish for flexible, purposeful work will all shape recruitment and retention. Under technological factors, online ordering, digital stock control and automated warehouses will need staff with digital skills and may reduce some manual roles. Under legal factors, changes in employment law, safety rules for forklifts and warehouses, and the data protection law for customer records will affect training and procedures. Under environmental factors, more demand for energy-efficient and hurricane-resistant building products will require staff who can advise customers on them. Each trend should be rated for likely impact and used to plan recruitment and training.
markingPoints: Relevant political and economic factors
Relevant social factors linked to the workforce
Relevant technological factors with skill effects
Relevant legal and environmental factors
Links the analysis to workforce planning or priorities

essays.stem: Explain how an organisation can turn its analysis of workforce trends into a training and development plan.
essays.modelAnswer: The organisation should start by listing the trends that most affect it and agreeing what each means in practice: for example, that 20% of supervisors will retire within five years, or that digital sales skills will be needed in every branch. It should then compare the skills and numbers it will need with those it has now, through a skills audit, to identify the gaps by role and by location. The gaps should be ranked by how urgent and important they are, using the strategic plan as a guide. For each priority gap, the organisation chooses the best response: training existing staff (upskilling), retraining staff whose roles are disappearing (reskilling), apprenticeships and partnerships with training providers, mentoring and succession plans for key posts, or recruiting from outside. The plan should state objectives, who will be trained, how, by when, the budget and who is responsible. It should link to national qualifications where possible, so that skills are recognised. Finally, the plan needs measures, such as the share of key posts with a ready successor, and should be reviewed each year as the trends change.
markingPoints: Identifies key trends and their practical meaning
Carries out a skills audit and gap analysis
Prioritises gaps against strategy
Chooses suitable responses with objectives, budget and responsibilities
Sets measures and reviews the plan

essays.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limits of using past trends to forecast future workforce needs, and explain how scenario planning can help.
essays.modelAnswer: Using past trends is a sensible starting point. The data is usually available, the method is simple to understand and explain, and patterns such as steady growth, seasonal peaks or retirements by age are often reliable over a short period. For example, if turnover has been about 15% for five years, it is reasonable to plan for a similar level next year. However, past trends have limits. They assume that the future will be like the past, but sudden changes, such as a new technology, a recession, a hurricane, a new law or a large new employer in the area, can break a trend. Forecasts become less reliable the further ahead they reach, and errors in old data carry forward. Scenario planning helps by preparing for several possible futures instead of one forecast. The organisation describes, for example, a high-growth, a steady and a low-growth scenario, works out the staff and skills each would need, and identifies actions that make sense in all of them, such as building digital skills. It also sets early warning signs that show which scenario is unfolding, so that plans can be adjusted quickly.
markingPoints: Gives strengths of trend-based forecasting
Gives limits such as sudden change or distance ahead
Uses a relevant example
Explains scenario planning clearly
Explains how scenarios help: robust actions and warning signs

practical1.title: Analyse a workforce data set and present trend charts with an interpretation
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a spreadsheet of five years of made-up workforce data for an organisation (for example a hotel group on the north coast, a call centre in Kingston or a parish health service), with staff numbers by department, age bands, leavers, vacancies, training hours and qualifications held. As a group, analyse the data and produce: a checked data sheet with any errors or gaps marked; a calculations sheet showing yearly growth, turnover rates, the share of staff over 55 and a three-year moving average of vacancies, each worked out and checked twice; at least four clear, labelled charts, each with a heading that says what it shows; a one-page interpretation of the main trends and their implications for workforce development; and a five-minute presentation to the assessor. Give each member a named role: data lead (checks and cleans the data), calculations analyst, chart designer, interpretation writer, and presenter (who also checks that the figures in the interpretation match the spreadsheet). In a group of four, the data lead also checks the interpretation's figures. Every member answers at least one question from the assessor.
materials: Spreadsheet of made-up workforce data from the assessor
Computers with spreadsheet and word-processing software
A screen or projector for the presentation
photos: The data sheet with errors and gaps marked
The four or more charts with their headings
The group presenting to the assessor
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the evidence
Errors and gaps in the data were found and handled sensibly
Growth, turnover, age share and moving average are correct
Charts suit the data and are clearly labelled
The interpretation separates trends from one-off changes and avoids false causes
Implications for workforce development are realistic
Explained their part and answered the assessor's question
safety: Use only the made-up data set; no real staff records
Treat the data as confidential and do not copy it off the Centre computers
Respect each member's view when agreeing the interpretation
Share the workload fairly and take short screen breaks

practical2.title: Research labour market trends for an industry and produce a workforce briefing
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group an industry (for example tourism and hospitality, business process outsourcing, construction or health care) and a research pack with extracts of made-up national labour market tables, a set of 30 job advertisements and short industry news items. The Centre's computers may also be used to view official public sources if the assessor allows. As a group, produce: a source table listing each source with its author, date, method and a reliability rating with reasons; a tally sheet of the skills asked for in the 30 job adverts, with the percentage of adverts asking for each skill worked out and checked twice; a PESTLE poster of the trends affecting the industry's workforce; two short scenarios for the industry five years from now; and a two-page briefing for a training provider recommending which skills and programmes to develop. Give each member a named role: source researcher (source table), job advert analyst (tally and percentages), PESTLE lead (poster), scenario planner, and briefing writer. In a group of four, the scenario planner also writes the scenarios into the briefing. Each member explains their part to the assessor.
materials: Research pack from the assessor: labour market extracts, 30 job adverts and news items
Computers with internet access (if allowed), spreadsheet and word-processing software
Poster paper, markers and sticky notes
photos: The source table with reliability ratings
The job advert tally sheet with percentages
The group explaining the briefing to the assessor
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the evidence
Sources are fairly judged for reliability, with reasons
The tally and percentages are accurate
PESTLE factors are relevant to the industry's workforce
The scenarios are plausible and different from each other
Explained their part clearly when asked
safety: Use only official or reputable sites and follow the Centre's internet rules
Do not copy text from sources; summarise in your own words and record the source
Do not collect personal details from job adverts
Share the work fairly and take short screen breaks
